q: A college wants the views of all its 600 students on a new online fee portal before the design starts, and it has only one week. Which way of gathering requirements suits this best?
o: An online questionnaire sent to every student
A one-to-one interview with every student
Writing the program first and asking students afterwards
Watching one student at the fee counter for a day
x: A questionnaire collects answers from a large group quickly and cheaply. Interviews give detail but 600 of them cannot be done in a week, and one student's view is too small a sample.

q: For a library management system, which of these is a functional requirement?
o: The system must show search results within 2 seconds
The system must let a member reserve a book that is currently issued
The system must run on computers with 4 GB of RAM
The system must be available 24 hours a day
x: A functional requirement says what the system must do (a service such as reserving a book). Speed, hardware and availability describe how well or where it works, so they are non-functional requirements.

q: During a feasibility study, a team compares the expected cost of building a new system with the money the system will save over the next few years. Which kind of feasibility is this?
x: Economic (financial) feasibility asks whether the benefits are worth the cost. Technical feasibility asks whether the hardware, software and skills are available, not whether it pays.

q: A project has four tasks. P takes 3 weeks and starts at once. Q takes 2 weeks and can start only after P ends. R takes 4 weeks and starts at the same time as P. S takes 1 week and can start only after both Q and R end. What is the shortest time to finish the project?
x: The chain P then Q ends after 3 + 2 = 5 weeks, while R running alongside ends after 4 weeks; S must wait for the later one, so it runs in week 6 and the project takes 5 + 1 = 6 weeks. 10 weeks adds all tasks as if none ran in parallel.

q: A project's cost estimate is Rs 800,000. The plan adds a contingency reserve of 15% of this amount for risks. What total budget should be requested?
Agile methods value which of these more than comprehensive documentation?
o: Formal sign-off at the end of each stage
x: Agile puts working software ahead of heavy documentation, and also values customer collaboration over contract negotiation and responding to change over following a plan. So contracts, fixed plans and stage sign-offs are the things Agile values less, not more.

q: Which is an advantage of the Waterfall model?
o: Users can change the requirements at any time at little cost
Users see a working part of the software every few weeks
Testing goes on from the first day of the project
Each stage ends with clear documents, so progress is easy to check
x: Waterfall finishes and documents one stage before the next begins, which makes it simple to plan and to measure progress. Cheap changes and frequent working releases are features of Agile, not Waterfall.

q: A hospital receives its new system, built with the Waterfall model, 14 months after the project began. The staff find that several screens do not match the way they actually work. Which weakness of Waterfall does this show?
o: Too many small releases confused the staff
Testing was done before the code was written
Users see working software only near the end, so misunderstandings are found late
x: In Waterfall the users mostly see the system after coding and testing are complete, so a misunderstood requirement surfaces late, when it is costly to fix. Waterfall does have a requirements stage at the very start, and frequent small releases belong to Agile.

q: In the Waterfall model, the documents produced in the design stage are mainly used as the input to which stage?
x: Each Waterfall stage feeds the next: programmers write the code from the design (flowcharts, data structures, screen layouts). Requirements analysis and the feasibility study come before design, not after it.

q: Why do software teams follow a Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)?
o: It divides the work into clear stages that can be planned, checked and managed
It removes the need to test the software
It lets coding start before anyone knows what is needed
It guarantees that the software has no errors
x: The SDLC gives a project an ordered set of stages, from requirements to maintenance, so work can be planned and tracked. It includes a testing stage and cannot promise error-free software.

q: A team copies its source code to a separate server at the end of every day. Which project risk does this mainly reduce?
o: A skilled team member leaving the project
Losing work if a developer's computer fails
The project going over its budget
x: A daily backup on another machine means a crashed or stolen computer costs at most one day of work. It does nothing about changing requirements, staff leaving or cost overruns, which need other risk plans.

q: Instead of inventing their own approach, a team uses a well-known, tested way of organising code so that many screens update automatically whenever the data changes. What are they using?
x: A design pattern is a proven, reusable solution to a common design problem, such as keeping many views in step with one set of data. A Gantt chart is a planning tool and a test case is used in testing.

q: An Agile team delivers 4 finished features at the end of every 2-week sprint. The product needs 18 features. At least how many weeks pass before all 18 are delivered?
x: 18 / 4 = 4.5, and a part sprint still takes a whole sprint, so 5 sprints are needed: 5 x 2 = 10 weeks. 9 weeks treats 4.5 sprints as possible; 8 weeks (4 sprints) delivers only 16 features.

q: A Gantt chart shows four tasks: T1 in weeks 1-3, T2 in weeks 4-6, T3 in weeks 5-8 and T4 in weeks 9-10. Which two tasks are in progress at the same time?
x: T2 runs to week 6 and T3 starts in week 5, so both are under way in weeks 5 and 6. T1 ends in week 3 just before T2 starts in week 4, so those two only meet end to start and do not overlap.

q: Which requirement is badly written, because it cannot be measured or tested?
o: The app must show a student's result within 3 seconds of a search
The app should be user-friendly and fast
The app must let a teacher enter marks from 0 to 100
The app must lock an account after 3 wrong passwords
x: "User-friendly" and "fast" mean different things to different people, so no test can show the requirement is met. The other three give exact numbers or actions that a tester can check.

q: During project planning, deciding how many programmers, testers and computers the project will need is called:
x: Resource planning works out the people, equipment and money each task needs. Debugging and regression testing happen during testing, and deployment comes at the end.

q: A project has two tasks done one after the other: design needs 6 person-months of work and coding needs 12 person-months. The same team of 3 programmers works on each task in turn, and the work divides evenly among them. How long does the project take?
x: Design takes 6 / 3 = 2 months and coding 12 / 3 = 4 months, one after the other: 2 + 4 = 6 months. 18 months forgets to share the work among the three programmers; 4 months counts only the coding.

q: In a Waterfall project, why does the client sign the requirements document before the design stage begins?
o: So that coding can begin before the design is drawn
So both sides agree on what will be built before later stages depend on it
So that no testing will be needed later
So that the requirements can be changed freely during coding
x: Every later Waterfall stage is built on the requirements, so they are fixed and agreed first; a change later means going back through the stages. Signing does not replace design or testing.

q:
What happens when this Python code runs?
```
marks = 72
print(mark + 5)
```
o: It stops with a runtime error (NameError), because `mark` has not been defined
It is a syntax error, because a bracket is missing
x: The variable created is marks, but line 2 uses mark, a name Python has never seen, so the program stops with a NameError when that line runs. The brackets are complete, so it is not a syntax error.

q:
What happens when this Python code runs?
```
age = 18
print("Age: " + age)
```
o: It is a syntax error at the `+` sign
It stops with a runtime error (TypeError), because a string and an integer cannot be joined with `+`
x: In Python, + between a str and an int raises a TypeError when the line runs; the number must be converted first, as in str(age). The line is written correctly, so it is not a syntax error.

q: A C program has a semicolon missing at the end of one statement. When is this error found?
o: Only when a user checks the output
When the program is compiled, so it cannot run
Never, because C ignores missing semicolons
x: A missing semicolon breaks the rules of the language, so it is a syntax error that the compiler reports, and no program is produced until it is fixed. Runtime errors, by contrast, appear only while the program runs.

q: A marks field should accept whole numbers from 0 to 100. A tester types `abc` into it to check that the program rejects it. What kind of test data is this?
x: Data that the program should refuse, such as letters in a number field, is invalid or erroneous test data. Boundary data would be values at the edges, such as 0, 100 or 101.

q:
This Python code should print the largest number in the list. What does it print, and what is wrong?
```
nums = [-4, -9, -2]
big = 0
for n in nums:
    if n > big:
        big = n
print(big)
```
o: It prints -2; the code is correct
It prints 0; a logic error, because `big` should start at `nums[0]`
It prints -9; the comparison is the wrong way round
It stops with a runtime error at `n > big`
x: Every number in the list is negative, so n > big (n > 0) is never true and big stays 0, which is not even in the list. The program runs without any error message, so this is a logic error; starting with big = nums[0] gives the correct -2.

q: A programmer adds lines such as `print("x =", x)` at several points in a program to watch how the values change while it runs. What is this?
o: Debugging by printing values at chosen points
x: Printing variables at chosen points lets the programmer see where a value first goes wrong, which is a simple debugging technique. Black-box and acceptance testing look only at inputs and outputs, not at values inside the code.

q: Before the official release, a company lets a group of real users outside the company try a nearly finished app and report the problems they meet. This is:
x: Beta testing is done by real users in their own setting just before release. Alpha testing is the earlier stage done inside the developer's own company, and unit testing checks single parts of the code.

q:
What happens when this Python program is run?
```
print("start")
x = 5
    y = x + 1
print(y)
```
o: Nothing is printed; Python reports an IndentationError, a syntax error, before running any line
start is printed, then an error is reported at line 3
x: Python checks the syntax of the whole file before running it, and line 3 is indented for no reason, so an IndentationError (a kind of syntax error) is reported and not even line 1 runs. Printing start first is what would happen with a runtime error.

q:
What happens when this Python program is run?
```
print("begin")
n = int("12x")
print(n * 2)
```
o: Nothing is printed, because it is a syntax error
begin is printed, then the program stops with a runtime error (ValueError)
x: The code is written correctly, so it starts and line 1 prints begin. Line 2 then fails while running because "12x" is not a whole number, giving a ValueError, so line 3 never runs.

q:
The programmer wanted this Python code to print the numbers 1 to 5. What is wrong with it?
```
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
```
o: A syntax error: the condition of `while` needs brackets
A logic error: `i` never changes, so 1 is printed again and again without end
A runtime error on the first line
x: The line i = i + 1 is missing, so i stays 1, i <= 5 is always true and the loop never ends. The code is valid Python (brackets round the condition are optional), so it is a logic error, not a syntax error.

q: A test case for a function normally records:
o: only the name of the programmer
the input values and the expected output
the time taken to compile the program
x: A test case states what to enter and what result should come out, so the actual result can be compared with it. Source code and programmer names do not tell a tester whether the function works.

q: In a debugger, running a program one statement at a time to see what each line does is called:
x: Stepping executes one line, then pauses so variables can be checked before the next line. Regression testing re-runs old tests after a change; it is not done line by line.
